rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. The first run's early last peak suggests sufficient time margin for this diagnostic.
Keep the successful shallower slope and test higher temperature to shift selectivity at the remaining near-coelution. This should also preserve or improve the last-peak time below 10 minutes.

Test an intermediate temperature to avoid the selectivity crossings seen between 40 and 55 C, with a slightly shallower gradient to spread the remaining close pairs. The predicted last peak is near 10 minutes, retaining most of the available time advantage.

Use a narrower solvent window to obtain a shallower slope while removing low-organic time before the main peak cluster. This targets the remaining close pair at 55 C while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Hold the improved gradient fixed and increase temperature one step to test selectivity of the only unresolved pair. All other pairs have useful resolution margins, and the last peak is comfortably below 10 minutes.

Make the gradient shallower at 60 C to improve the newly limiting pair, while checking that the early cluster remains resolved. The current 7.80-minute last peak leaves room for this increase in gradient duration.

The limiting pair appears to cross as the gradient becomes shallower; move farther past that crossing to recover separation. Raise the starting organic fraction slightly to offset the longer gradient and aim to keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Reverse the slope change because the shallower gradient moved the limiting pair toward coelution. A lower starting organic fraction should help preserve separation in the early cluster while the steeper slope separates the later critical pair.

Shorten the best gradient by one grid step to move the later critical pair farther from its slope-induced crossing. The early cluster has some resolution margin, so this may improve both the score and elution time.

This gives a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, just above injection 10's 0.04444, targeting the pair at R = 1.49 without exhausting the early pairs' margins. The final organic fraction remains above the observed elution window, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Injection 11 reaches the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark and test a slightly steeper slope for faster fully resolved elution. This small increase probes the narrow resolution margins in the early cluster.

Retain injection 11 as the maximum-score benchmark and test whether a lower starting organic fraction protects the early critical pairs under a steeper gradient. This explores another route to fully resolved, rapid elution without repeating a method.

Raise both gradient endpoints by one step while preserving slope to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature method. This tests whether injection 16's resolution margins can tolerate removing some initial low-organic retention.
